en: They cried out in tears,
The children of the Muslim people.
When the two giants came in,
Ruling Andijan,
A khan like Aykojo died,
And sixty champions died as well.
The sovereign with the mighty ancestral spirit
Watched from a hill,
His battle cry splitting stone.
Bakay at his side
He kept troubling,
Saying, 'Joust with those two.'
At that time the Gray Belt
Descended from the sky.
When he cried out and fastened it at his waist,
To the dearly born lord
The Forty Hidden Saints became companions.
When he shouted and fastened it at his waist,
The White Holy Man came and offered his hand.
When he journeyed on a distant road,
Six saints opened the way.
The merciless strife,
Had she not brought it with her?
Weeping piteously to the one God,
Dedicating it to her precious Semetey,
Had she not brought it with her?
Saying, 'Leaving it behind would be hard,'
Saying, 'It is an object left by his father Manas,'
Weeping piteously to the one God,
Dedicating it to her forlorn Semetey,
Had she not brought it with her?
The Gray Belt left by her lord Manas
She fitted snugly at her waist,
Concealing that she was a woman.
Your dear sister-in-law Kanykey
Now became a man.
Your precious, unfortunate sister-in-law,
Grieving for her dead husband,
Dressed herself in men's clothes.
The eight khans lying ahead,
She knew, would become enemies.
Almambet's Syrbarang
She hung across her shoulder blades.
Almambet's Syrbarang—
Let me tell of Syrbarang.
When one went out with Syrbarang slung on,
It was the mirror of one's shoulder blades;
When one entered a clash with the enemy,
It was solace for one's entrusted soul.
With thick muzzle, Apple-Head,
Not distinguishing far from near,
Not breaking down in twelve days,
Almambet's Syrbarang
She hung across her shoulder blades.
Inside a rawhide saddlebag,
The never-diminishing ammunition
She loaded onto Akborchuk.
The bright-red steel Lacquered Spear
She took up at a slant.
The helmet of blue iron
She lifted and put on her head.
The banner swayed in her hand,
All the keen steel equipment
Flashing in its proper place.
No one could recognize her as a woman.
Tall of body, broad of shoulder,
Both champion and lion,
Racing a horse while a widow,
Your accomplished sister-in-law was this hero.
Taytoru, who would race,
With hoe-like hooves and broad rump,
Was a steed of the open country.
Saying, 'I entrust it to fate,' without pausing,
Your mountain-like sister-in-law
Of the courser Taytoru
Tied the forelock with blue silk,
And bound his tail with white silk.
Your sister-in-law with the hero's frame
A great lead rope two fathoms long
Selected and fastened on.
A white halter braided in the okoro pattern,
A halter fitting Taytoru,
She chose a strong one and secured it.
Your sister-in-law led him tirelessly.
Akborchuk beneath her
She rode at a gallop like a sheep.
Taking a shortcut along a narrow path,
Before the eight khans in Bukhara,
Your sister-in-law brought him, leading him.
Looking neither up nor down,
Your sister-in-law never thought, 'I shall die.'
Without looking around,
Your sister-in-law did not spare her life at all.
She resolved to start trouble.
If someone interfered with her horse,
Your sister-in-law resolved to make a spectacle.
Her breast could not contain her many cares;
Your sister-in-law's tears streamed in ten directions.
"This very year my elder is ninety-five,
My saint who bore a mountain-like sovereign.
At the sight of her, my heart is content.
I have no Mecca but my mother.
My river, whose expanse is like a lake,
Whom I carried on my broad back,
My saint whom I brought from Talas.
When I cherish her, my belly is full.
I have no Mecca but my mother.
My venerable white lady,
Let me go to my mother,
Let me receive my mother's blessing.
My venerable white lady, my sacred mother,
Let me go to my mother.
If my mother does not give her blessing,
Why should I race Taytoru?
Without receiving my mother's blessing,
How can I go to Bukhara?"
Bending from horseback,
From Akborchuk's back,
Your noble sister-in-law Kanykey
Leaped down and ran.
Speaking softly in anguish,
Calling her 'Mother,' she pleaded:
"My river, great as a mountain,
From my honored Kyrgyz people,
Carrying you on my broad back,
My saint whom I brought here.
At the sight of you, my heart is content.
My venerable white lady, my sacred mother,
I have no Mecca but you!
Valiant mother, listen.
I have no support to lean on.
If I race Taytoru for a prize,
My renowned Kyrgyz people are not here!
Who would show kindness
To a widow like me?
Let me race to divine my fate,
Mother, my steed Taytoru.
If Taytoru comes through,
I shall see some good fortune.
The countless prizes in Bukhara,
Mother, I shall divide by the measure of a whip.
The only one left by your Slayer son,
This year, mother, I shall see with my own eyes.
I shall send word to your people.
On the only one left by my khan,
I shall place my golden crown,
And seat him on the golden throne.
To this Bukhara here,
This year I shall raise him as khan.
If Taytoru falls behind,
A dreadful day will fall upon my head.
I shall suffer, my thoughts torn apart;
I shall shed my own blood.
For sixty sheep and forty yearlings,
The Aktinte that I bought
I shall draw from its sheath.
Today this accursed soul of mine
I shall offer up as a sacrifice.
I shall die in suffering.
Mother, today I shall see the face of Judgment!
Give me your blessing; let me receive it.
Before my sovereign father,
Let me go like a man.
If Taytoru comes through,
If the true divine power supports me,
In this Bukhara here
Let me make a spectacle.
Do not withhold your prayer from me,
My mother, like a prophet;
Do not withhold your blessing from me!"
The venerable white lady Chyiyrdy
Raised her hands, spreading them wide,
Coughing with deep, repeated coughs.
Saying, 'Allah!' she raised her hands,
And wept again, saying, 'Creator!'
She wept piteously to the one God,
Raising her hands, weeping piteously.
To Manas, gone to the other world,
She wept again, saying, 'Give support!'
"Ajybay and Bakay, you two khans,
Give support in every undertaking.
My dear one God,
Make my child Kanykey's undertaking prosper!
Almambet and Chubak, my twins,
Look upon my widow.
Syrgak and Serek, my oceans,
Urge on this sister-in-law of yours!
Sixty kinds of guardian spirit,
Forty-two Khizr-Ilyases,
God, make her undertaking prosper;
Support my widow!
My poor widowed child,
My dear one God,
If you created her as a living soul,
Do not make her hang her head!
God, do not let a bird of prey eat the swan.
This child of mine who goes about sobbing,
If you created her as a living soul,
In this Bukhara here,
Do not let them call her a ruined woman!
O God, do not let a bird of prey eat the goose.
This child of mine, Kanykey,
If you created her as a living soul,
In this Bukhara here,
Do not let them call her a fugitive woman.
O Kanykey, my foal,
May God grant your wish;
This Taytoru of yours,
May he come through in Bukhara!
May God grant your wish;
May God lift your sorrow;
May God relieve your grief!"
Your mourning sister-in-law Kanykey,
Receiving her mother Chyiyrdy's blessing,
Kanykey, the wife of Manas,
Mounted and set out toward Bukhara,
Taking a direct route through the foothills.
Your mother led Taytoru,
Her banner fluttering,
All her equipment
Flashing along her body.
Those who saw her were unsettled.
In appearance and bearing,
She looked like hero Manas of old.
A black-spotted leopard
Raged at her side,
Your dear, fierce sister-in-law
It supported invisibly.
A short-tailed spotted lion,
Raging close beside her,
Gave its support as well.
When your sister-in-law grew wrathful,
Her very tidings could take one's life.
If you looked upon her face,
Between her two cheeks
Grew enough hair for a felt sock.
Flame hissed from her mouth.
Her formidable teeth, like a gate,
Scattered like grains of millet.
Flame poured from her mouth;
She looked like an enormous mountain.
When she entered Bukhara,
The eight khans in Bukhara
Were deeply troubled.
In appearance and bearing,
Your sister-in-law looked like a devouring monster.
Not knowing she was a woman,
The eight khans in Bukhara
Split apart and scurried away.
With both hands upon their breasts,
All cried out greetings.
Their white-turbaned khojas,
Their mullahs who studied sacred lessons,
All their long-eared ones,
Their elders with grizzled beards—
Not just one of them,
